title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: Our platform strategy—connecting consumers, earners, and merchants across Mobility and Delivery—is driving deeper engagement than any single-vertical competitor can match.
epigraph.author: Dara Khosrowshahi, FY2025 Earnings Release

web_blocks.html: Uber runs three main business units: Mobility, Delivery, and Freight [1, 3]. Two cross-platform tools support them: Uber One and Uber Advertising. In FY2025, total revenue hit $52,017 million (+18% YoY) on $193.5 billion in Gross Bookings [1, 2]. Full-year Adjusted EBITDA reached $8,730 million [1, 2]. In Q3 2026, quarterly Gross Bookings climbed to $59.82 billion (+20% YoY) [3]. Quarterly Adjusted EBITDA hit $2.96 billion, or 5.0% of Gross Bookings, showing steady margin gains across both core apps [3].

1. Mobility ($29,670M FY2025 Revenue, 57.0% mix): Mobility matches riders with drivers across UberX, Comfort, Black, and Reserve [1]. It also runs two-wheelers like Uber Moto in growth markets and driverless cars with Waymo in Austin and Atlanta [16, 18]. Uber targets ~700 driverless cars on its app by late 2026 and over 2,000 in 2027 [16]. Mobility revenue rose 18% YoY in FY2025 on strong trip growth, airport rides, Uber for Teens, and Shuttle [1]. Because Uber acts as an agent in most markets, net revenue reflects its fee after driver pay, plus pass-through items.

web_blocks.caption: Uber Segment Revenue, Gross Bookings & Adjusted EBITDA Mix (FY2025 & Q3 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Mobility remains the primary profit engine (~90% of consolidated Adjusted EBITDA before corporate overhead), while Delivery has scaled into a $100B+ Gross Bookings and ~$3.57B Adjusted EBITDA powerhouse [1, 2, 3].

web_blocks.html: 2. Delivery ($17,250M FY2025 Revenue, 33.2% mix): Delivery moves meals, groceries, and retail goods via Uber Eats and Uber Direct [1]. Revenue jumped 25% YoY in FY2025 while segment Adjusted EBITDA rose ~45% YoY [1]. Delivery Gross Bookings crossed a $100 billion yearly run-rate for the first time [2]. Delivery also drives most of Uber Advertising, which topped a $2.5 billion yearly run-rate in 2026 [19]. Sponsored Listings now exceed 2% of Delivery Gross Bookings, aided by high-impact Journey Takeovers [19]. Meanwhile, Uber One passed 50 million members and drives over half of combined Mobility and Delivery Gross Bookings [3, 5]. Members spend about 3x more each month than non-members and stay on the app much longer.

3. Freight ($5,100M FY2025 Revenue, 9.8% mix): Uber Freight is a digital B2B truck broker and supply-chain tool [1]. It grew from the 2021 Transplace deal and links large shippers with trucking firms. After a long U.S. freight slump (-1% YoY revenue and ~$(33)M Adjusted EBITDA in FY2025), Freight bounced back in Q3 2026 [1, 3]. Q3 2026 Freight Gross Bookings jumped 35% YoY to $1.77 billion [3]. Unlike Mobility and Delivery, Uber acts as principal broker in Freight and books the full shipping bill as revenue.

Cross-selling across apps sets Uber apart from single-app peers. Uber Direct lets shops sell on their own websites while using Uber couriers for last-mile delivery [1]. That fills mid-afternoon gaps when meal orders slow down, with zero consumer ad spend. At the same time, Sponsored Listings add ~90%-margin ad dollars on top of standard merchant fees [19]. Uber One ties the loop together by giving members $0 delivery fees and 6% Uber Cash back on rides [5]. A user who joins for Friday dinner stays for Monday airport rides.

Restaurant owners stay on Uber Eats because of simple kitchen math. Most shops already pay fixed rent, kitchen staff, and utility bills. An extra Uber Eats order uses spare kitchen capacity at high contribution margin, even after a 15%–25% fee. Adding a $1.80 Sponsored Listing click puts a local shop at the top of search results during peak dinner hours [19]. Uber captures multiple revenue streams from one merchant without raising consumer delivery fees.

Together, these three units form a balanced flywheel. Mobility brings high-margin urban cash flow, Delivery builds daily order habit and ad scale, and Freight adds enterprise shipping ties [1, 3]. Each unit shares core routing, payments, and fraud tools across the same platform.

web_blocks.title: Concrete End-to-End Walkthroughs: Consumer, Merchant, Driver & Shipper Economics
paragraphs: Mobility Walkthrough (Chicago O'Hare Airport Trip): A consultant lands at O'Hare at 6:15 PM and opens Uber. Holding Uber One, she earns 6% Uber Cash back and priority matching. Upfront pricing quotes $54.00 for a 19-mile Uber Comfort ride downtown; Uber's dispatch engine matches a driver 4 minutes away who just dropped off a departing passenger (minimizing unpaid deadhead miles). Out of the $54.00 gross fare, ~$36.50 goes to the driver, ~$4.50 covers state/airport fees and commercial auto insurance reserves, and ~$13.00 is recognized as Uber net Mobility revenue.

Delivery + Merchant Economics Walkthrough (Friday Dinner + Ad Monetization): A family in Austin opens Uber Eats at 7:30 PM. At the top of the search feed for 'Thai food', a local restaurant pays $1.80 per click for a Sponsored Listing placement—pure ~90%+ margin ad revenue for Uber [19]. The family orders $62.00 of food, pays $0 delivery fee via Uber One, and tips $8.00. On the merchant side, the restaurant pays a tiered marketplace commission (~15%–25% depending on marketing tier) on the $62.00 basket—worth paying because incremental off-premise orders utilize idle kitchen capacity without adding rent. A courier finishing a nearby drop-off bundles the pickup. Uber collects the merchant commission, consumer service fee, and ad click, netting ~$11.50 in revenue while paying the courier base fare plus 100% of the tip.

Freight Walkthrough (Midwest Pallet Load): A packaged-goods manufacturer needs 42,000 lbs of beverage pallets moved from Columbus, Ohio to Indianapolis on 24 hours' notice. Using Uber Freight's enterprise portal, the shipper posts the load at a dynamic market rate of $950. Uber Freight's algorithm matches an independent owner-operator whose truck is unloading 15 miles away, eliminating an empty backhaul. Uber Freight books $950 in Gross Bookings (and revenue, as principal broker), pays the carrier ~$825, and retains ~$125 gross margin to cover brokerage operations.

book_paragraphs: To see how Uber actually makes money, you have to stop thinking of it as a single taxi app and look at three distinct businesses sharing one massive logistics brain. In fiscal 2025, Uber generated $52.0 billion in revenue across $193.5 billion of Gross Bookings. By the third quarter of 2026, quarterly Gross Bookings alone hit $59.8 billion, putting the platform on an annualized run-rate well north of $230 billion.

Let's walk through all three segments with real-world examples so the accounting comes alive. First is Mobility—still the crown jewel, representing 57% of revenue ($29.67 billion in FY2025) and roughly $7.9 billion in segment Adjusted EBITDA. Imagine you step out of Chicago O'Hare on a rainy Tuesday evening. You tap Uber Comfort, see an upfront price of $54, and within four minutes a driver who just dropped off a departing flyer pulls up. Behind the scenes, Uber's matching engine minimized the driver's unpaid 'deadhead' miles, set aside a slice for commercial auto insurance and airport fees, paid the driver roughly two-thirds of the fare, and kept the net take rate as Mobility revenue.

What makes Mobility even stickier today is the breadth of product tiers layered onto that same driver supply. If you are a corporate traveler, you can pre-book an Uber Reserve ride 48 hours ahead for a guaranteed airport pickup at a higher take rate. If you are a parent, you can put your teenager on Uber for Teens with live trip tracking. And in cities like Austin and Atlanta, your next Uber Comfort match might not have a human driver at all—it might be a Waymo autonomous vehicle plugged directly into Uber's dispatch network.

book_subsections.title: Delivery, Merchant Economics & The Uber One Retention Math
paragraphs: Second is Delivery, which brought in $17.25 billion in FY2025 revenue (33.2% of the total) and ~$3.57 billion in Adjusted EBITDA—up 45% year-over-year as Delivery Gross Bookings crossed a $100 billion annual run-rate. Picture a Friday night in Austin: you open Uber Eats to order Thai food. Before you even scroll, the first restaurant you see paid Uber for a Sponsored Listing. Because you subscribe to Uber One—one of more than 50 million members who now drive over half of Uber's combined Mobility and Delivery bookings—you pay zero delivery fee.

Now look at that transaction from the restaurant owner's seat. The owner already pays fixed rent, kitchen staff, and utilities. An incremental $62 delivery order uses spare kitchen capacity, so even after paying Uber a 15% to 25% marketplace commission—plus $1.80 for a Sponsored Listing click to jump to the top of search—the incremental contribution margin is cash-flow positive. Better yet, merchants can also tap Uber Direct for white-label delivery on their own websites, turning Uber into an invisible logistics utility.

That is why Uber's advertising business scaled past a $2.5 billion annualized run-rate across Sponsored Listings and full-screen Journey Takeovers. And Uber One glues the entire consumer loop together: once you pay for Uber One to get zero-dollar delivery fees on Friday night, you naturally open Uber instead of a rival on Monday morning to earn 6% Uber Cash back on your airport ride. Members spend roughly three times more per month than non-members and churn far less than single-app users.

book_subsections.title: Freight: Principal Accounting vs. Marketplace Brokerage
paragraphs: Third is Uber Freight, representing $5.10 billion in FY2025 revenue (9.8% of the mix) and roughly breakeven profitability during the 2024–2025 trucking downturn, before rebounding 35% in Q3 2026 Gross Bookings. Instead of moving people or pad thai, Freight moves 40,000-pound pallets between warehouses—matching a beverage shipper in Columbus with an independent trucker looking for a return load to Indianapolis.

Unlike Mobility and Delivery, where Uber acts as an agent and records only its net fee as revenue, in Freight Uber acts as the principal broker and records the entire $950 freight bill as revenue while recording the $825 carrier payout inside Cost of Revenue. That accounting distinction explains why Freight looks bigger on the top line than in profit dollars, while still giving Uber deep enterprise relationships with Fortune 500 supply chains.

book_subsections.title: Deeper Analytical Synthesis
paragraphs: Another underappreciated piece of Delivery is Uber Direct—Uber's white-label delivery service for merchants who want to own the customer relationship on their own website or app while outsourcing the last-mile logistics to Uber's couriers. When a national pharmacy, grocer, or restaurant chain plugs into Uber Direct, Uber earns a fulfillment fee with zero consumer marketing spend and keeps its couriers busy during mid-afternoon lulls between lunch and dinner.

Put all three segments together—Mobility's $29.67 billion high-margin engine, Delivery's $17.25 billion scale and $2.5 billion-plus advertising machine, and Freight's $5.10 billion enterprise brokerage—and you see why Uber's platform is so hard to replicate piece by piece. A standalone rideshare app cannot cross-sell dinner; a standalone food app cannot cross-sell airport rides; and neither can match the habit loop of 50 million Uber One subscribers.

book_subsections.title: Institutional Takeaway & Risk Discipline
paragraphs: Take a step back and look at how the three segments reinforce one another in daily life. In the morning, Mobility carries commuters to offices and travelers to airports like Chicago O'Hare, generating ~$7.9 billion of annual Adjusted EBITDA on $29.67 billion of revenue. At lunch and dinner, Delivery brings meals, groceries, and retail packages to families in cities like Austin, generating $17.25 billion of revenue, ~$3.57 billion of Adjusted EBITDA, and over $2.5 billion in annualized high-margin advertising.

And between those peak windows, Uber Direct and Uber Freight keep the logistics engine humming—moving white-label retail orders and 40,000-pound B2B pallets across highways. Even though Freight accounts for less than 10% of revenue ($5.10 billion in FY2025) and acts as a principal broker booking gross freight bills, its 35% Gross Bookings rebound in Q3 2026 shows its cyclical optionality when trucking demand tightens.

Above all, Uber One is the glue that turns occasional app users into habitual multi-product subscribers. When 50 million-plus members generate more than half of combined Mobility and Delivery Gross Bookings and spend roughly three times more per month than non-members, customer acquisition costs drop and lifetime value compounds.

When you put Mobility, Delivery, and Freight together under one corporate roof, the strategic logic becomes unmistakable. Mobility supplies the high-frequency consumer habit and ~$7.9 billion in segment Adjusted EBITDA; Delivery supplies the $100 billion-plus frequency flywheel, Uber One lock-in, and $2.5 billion-plus advertising engine; and Freight gives Uber a seat at the table with enterprise supply chains across North America.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: AGENT VS. PRINCIPAL ACCOUNTING
book_callouts.text: Never compare segment revenues at face value without checking revenue recognition. Mobility and Delivery record net take-rate revenue (roughly 17% to 29% of Gross Bookings), whereas Freight records gross freight bills. That is why Mobility generates nearly $8 billion of Adjusted EBITDA on $30 billion of revenue while Freight hovers near breakeven on $5 billion.
